nameStory: The turkey vulture gets its name from its distinctive red, featherless head that resembles a wild turkey's head and neck. Early European settlers in North America noticed this striking similarity and the name stuck, even though these birds are not related to turkeys at all!
description: Turkey vultures are large, dark birds of prey that spend their days soaring high overhead in search of dead animals to eat. These impressive scavengers have wingspans that can reach six feet across and weigh about as much as a small cat. Their most distinctive feature is their bright red, bald head that contrasts sharply with their dark brown-black feathers. You'll most often see them gracefully riding air currents with their wings held in a shallow V-shape.

idTips.label: Wing Shape in Flight
idTips.description: Wings held in a distinctive shallow V-shape (called a dihedral) while soaring, never flat like a hawk. The wings appear long and broad with silvery flight feathers visible from below.

idTips.label: Red Bald Head
idTips.description: Adults have a bright red, completely featherless head and neck that looks wrinkled and rough, like old leather. Young birds have darker, grayish heads.

idTips.label: Flight Pattern
idTips.description: Soars with minimal wing flapping, often rocking or tilting from side to side as it rides air currents. Flies lower than most other large birds when searching for food.

idTips.label: Size and Color
idTips.description: Large bird with dark brown-black plumage that can look almost black from a distance. Body appears heavy but flies with surprising grace.

idTips.label: Voice
idTips.description: Rarely makes sound, but when threatened or disturbed, produces low hissing sounds or guttural grunts rather than typical bird calls.

idTips.label: Ground Behavior
idTips.description: Walks awkwardly on the ground with a hunched posture. Often seen with wings spread wide while sunbathing or drying off.

habitat: Turkey vultures prefer open areas where they can easily spot carrion from above, including farmlands, pastures, roadsides, and forest edges throughout New England. They need areas with good air currents for soaring, so you'll often see them over valleys, ridgelines, and open hills. They roost communally in large trees, abandoned buildings, or rocky outcrops, often returning to the same spots night after night.

seasonality.spring: Turkey vultures return to New England in March and April, often seen in small groups riding warming air currents. This is when they're most active in courtship and selecting nesting sites in secluded areas.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity season with adults feeding young and frequently soaring during warm afternoons when thermals are strongest. Large numbers may gather at abundant food sources.
seasonality.fall: Groups begin gathering for migration in September and October, with impressive kettles of dozens or hundreds of vultures spiraling upward before heading south. Most have departed by November.
seasonality.winter: Rare in New England during winter months, though occasional individuals may overwinter during mild years, especially in southern areas near reliable food sources.

funFact: Turkey vultures have an incredibly powerful sense of smell and can detect the scent of death from over a mile away - they're one of the few birds that rely more on smell than sight to find food, and they can smell a dead mouse hidden under a forest canopy!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with black vultures (which have shorter, wider wings held flat) and eagles (which hold wings flat and have feathered heads). Remember: Turkey vultures are the only large, dark soaring bird that holds its wings in a V-shape and rocks back and forth while flying.
contextualKnowledge: Despite their name, turkey vultures are not related to turkeys at all - they're not even closely related to the vultures of Europe, Africa, and Asia. This is a perfect example of convergent evolution, where unrelated species develop similar traits to fill the same ecological role as nature's cleanup crew.
compareHints: Turkey vultures are the only member of their genus in New England, making them unique among our region's vultures. Compared to black vultures (the only other vulture species in New England), turkey vultures are larger, have longer wings, hold their wings in a V-shape rather than flat, and have the distinctive red head as adults. Turkey vultures also rock more noticeably in flight and are much more common throughout the region.
